Introduction\\\\n\\\\nResearch in the field of physically based animation in computer graphics is concerned with finding new methods for\\\\nthe simulation of physical phenomena such as the dynamics\\\\nof rigid bodies, deformable objects or fluid flow. In contrast\\\\nto computational sciences where the main focus is on accuracy, the main issues here are stability, robustness and speed\\\\nwhile the results should remain visually plausible. Therefore, existing methods from computational sciences can not\\\\nbe adopted one to one. In fact, the main justification for\\\\ndoing research on physically based simulation in computer\\\\ngraphics is to come up with specialized methods, tailored to\\\\nthe particular needs in the field. The method we present falls\\\\ninto this category.\\\\n\\\\nThe traditional approach to simulating dynamic objects\\\\nhas been to work with forces. At the beginning of each time\\\\nstep, internal and external forces are accumulated. Examples\\\\nof internal forces are elastic forces in deformable objects or\\\\nviscosity and pressure forces in fluids. Gravity and collision\\\\nforces are examples of external forces. Newton’s second law\\\\nof motion relates forces to accelerations via the mass. So us-\\\\n\\\\ning the density or lumped masses of vertices, the forces are\\\\ntransformed into accelerations. Any time integration scheme\\\\ncan then be used to first compute the velocities from the accelerations and then the positions from the velocities. Some\\\\napproaches use impulses instead of forces to control the animation. Because impulses directly change velocities, one\\\\nlevel of integration can be skipped.\\\\n\\\\nIn computer graphics and especially in computer games\\\\nit is often desirable to have direct control over positions of\\\\nobjects or vertices of a mesh. The user might want to attach\\\\na vertex to a kinematic object or make sure the vertex always\\\\nstays outside a colliding object. The method we propose here\\\\nworks directly on positions which makes such manipulations easy. In addition, with the position based approach it is\\\\npossible to control the integration directly thereby avoiding\\\\novershooting and energy gain problems in connection with\\\\nexplicit integration. So the main features and advantages of\\\\nposition based dynamics are\\\\n\\\\n*•* Position based simulation gives control over explicit integration and removes the typical instability problems.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n**Figure 1:** *A known deformation benchmark test, applied here to a cloth character under pressure.*\\\\n\\\\n*•* Positions of vertices and parts of objects can directly be\\\\nmanipulated during the simulation.\\\\n\\\\n*•* The formulation we propose allows the handling of general constraints in the position based setting.\\\\n\\\\n*•* The explicit position based solver is easy to understand\\\\nand implement.\\\\n\\\\n## 2. Related Work\\\\n\\\\nThe recent state of the art report [NMK<sup>∗</sup> 05] gives a good\\\\noverview of the methods used in computer graphics to simulate deformable objects, e.g. mass-spring systems, the finite\\\\nelement method or finite difference approaches. Abstract\\n\\n*The most popular approaches for the simulation of dynamic systems in computer graphics are force based. Internal\\nand external forces are accumulated from which accelerations are computed based on Newton’s second law of\\nmotion. A time integration method is then used to update the velocities and finally the positions of the object.*\\n*A few simulation methods (most rigid body simulators) use impulse based dynamics and directly manipulate\\nvelocities. In this paper we present an approach which omits the velocity layer as well and immediately works\\non the positions. The main advantage of a position based approach is its controllability. Overshooting problems\\nof explicit integration schemes in force based systems can be avoided. In addition, collision constraints can be\\nhandled easily and penetrations can be resolved completely by projecting points to valid locations. We have used\\nthe approach to build a real time cloth simulator which is part of a physics software library for games. Introduction\\n\\nResearch in the field of physically based animation in computer graphics is concerned with finding new methods for\\nthe simulation of physical phenomena such as the dynamics\\nof rigid bodies, deformable objects or fluid flow. In contrast\\nto computational sciences where the main focus is on accuracy, the main issues here are stability, robustness and speed\\nwhile the results should remain visually plausible. Therefore, existing methods from computational sciences can not\\nbe adopted one to one. In fact, the main justification for\\ndoing research on physically based simulation in computer\\ngraphics is to come up with specialized methods, tailored to\\nthe particular needs in the field. The method we present falls\\ninto this category.\\n\\nThe traditional approach to simulating dynamic objects\\nhas been to work with forces. At the beginning of each time\\nstep, internal and external forces are accumulated. Examples\\nof internal forces are elastic forces in deformable objects or\\nviscosity and pressure forces in fluids. Gravity and collision\\nforces are examples of external forces. Newton’s second law\\nof motion relates forces to accelerations via the mass. So us-\\n\\ning the density or lumped masses of vertices, the forces are\\ntransformed into accelerations. Any time integration scheme\\ncan then be used to first compute the velocities from the accelerations and then the positions from the velocities. Some\\napproaches use impulses instead of forces to control the animation. Because impulses directly change velocities, one\\nlevel of integration can be skipped.\\n\\nIn computer graphics and especially in computer games\\nit is often desirable to have direct control over positions of\\nobjects or vertices of a mesh. The user might want to attach\\na vertex to a kinematic object or make sure the vertex always\\nstays outside a colliding object. The method we propose here\\nworks directly on positions which makes such manipulations easy. In addition, with the position based approach it is\\npossible to control the integration directly thereby avoiding\\novershooting and energy gain problems in connection with\\nexplicit integration. So the main features and advantages of\\nposition based dynamics are\\n\\n*•* Position based simulation gives control over explicit integration and removes the typical instability problems.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**Figure 1:** *A known deformation benchmark test, applied here to a cloth character under pressure.*\\n\\n*•* Positions of vertices and parts of objects can directly be\\nmanipulated during the simulation.\\n\\n*•* The formulation we propose allows the handling of general constraints in the position based setting.\\n\\n*•* The explicit position based solver is easy to understand\\nand implement.\\n\\n## 2. Related Work\\n\\nThe recent state of the art report [NMK<sup>∗</sup> 05] gives a good\\noverview of the methods used in computer graphics to simulate deformable objects, e.g. mass-spring systems, the finite\\nelement method or finite difference approaches. Apart from\\nthe citation of [MHTG05], position based dynamics does not\\nappear in this survey. However, parts of the position based\\napproach have appeared in various papers without naming it\\nexplicitly and without defining a complete framework.\\n\\nJakobsen [Jak01] built his *Fysix* engine on a position\\nbased approach. His central idea was to use a Verlet integrator and manipulate positions directly. Because velocities\\nare implicitly stored by current and the previous positions,\\nthe velocities are implicitly updated by the position manipulation. While he focused mainly on distance constraints,\\nhe only gave vague hints on how more general constraints\\ncould be handled. In this paper we present a fully general\\napproach which handles general constraints. We also focus\\non the important issue of conservation of linear and angular momenta by position projection. We work with explicit\\nvelocities instead of storing previous positions which makes\\ndamping and friction simulation much easier.\\n\\nDesbrun [DSB99] and Provot [Pro95] use constraint projection in mass spring systems to prevent springs from overstretching. In contrast to a full position based approach, projection is only used as a polishing process for those springs\\nthat are stretched too much and not as the basic simulation\\nmethod.\\n\\nBridson *et al.* use a traditional force based approach for\\n\\ncloth simulation [BFA02] and combine it with a geometric collision resolving algorithm based on positions to make\\nsure that the collision resolving impulses are kept within stable bounds. The same holds for the kinematical collision correction step proposed by Volino *et al.* [VCMT95].\\n\\nA position based approach has been used by Clavet *et\\nal.* [CBP05] to simulate viscoelastic fluids. Their approach\\nis not fully position based because the time step appears in\\nvarious places of their position projections. Thus, the integration is only conditionally stable as regular explicit integration.\\n\\nMüller *et al.* [MHTG05] simulate deformable objects\\nby moving points towards certain goal positions which are\\nfound by matching the rest state to the current state of the\\nobject. Their integration method is the closest to the one we\\npropose here. They only treat one specialized global constraint and, therefore, do not need a position solver.\\n\\nFedor [Fed05] uses Jakobsen’s approach to simulate characters in games. His method is tuned to the particular problem of simulating human characters. He uses several skeletal\\nrepresentations and keeps them in sync via projections.\\n\\nFaure [Fau98] uses a Verlet integration scheme by modifying the positions rather than the velocities. New positions\\nare computed by linearizing the constraints while we work\\nwith the non linear constraint functions directly.\\n\\nWe define general constraints via a constraint function\\nas [BW98] and [THMG04].
